newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia wants OPEC to maintain output ceiling.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia wants OPEC to maintain output ceiling.

text.p: Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana said Indonesia wanted the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to maintain its current output ceiling of 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd).
"Yes, we want OPEC to roll over its ceiling of 25.03 million through the end of the year," Sudjana told Reuters late on Friday night.

Indonesia's position on the output ceiling is consistent with that of most OPEC members including Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, in order to avoid sending any unexpected signals to vulnerable oil markets.

But while OPEC ministers will focus on efforts to curb a sharp slide in world oil prices, traders say they expect few surprises and see further market weakness whatever the outcome of the meeting in Vienna on June 25.

Prices on the world benchmark Brent blend crude plunged to a 13-month low of $17.38 per barrel last week before recovering to close at $17.63 per barrel on Friday on London's International Petroleum Exchange.
Sudjana also said Indonesia would like to see Iraq's 1.2 million bpd quota to remain unchanged for the time being.
"I think Iraq's quota at this moment should be maintained," he said.
Early this month, Iraq told OPEC it produced and supplied to the market 1.489 million bpd in May, well below April's 1.7 million bpd, but still in excess of its OPEC quota.

Last month, the United Nations renewed an oil-for-food deal with Iraq allowing Baghdad to sell another $2 billion worth of oil over six months to raise money for humanitarian imports. Sudjana urged the 11 OPEC member countries to stick to their current quotas to avoid a fall in the price of oil.
"OPEC members must stick to their quota because if not, all of us will become victims of the price fall. Although it is difficult because many members have their own interests," he said.

Sudjana said Indonesia has a proposal to take to the OPEC ministerial meeting on June 25, but he declined to give any details. "There is something that Indonesia will propose but I don't want to talk about it now," he said.
He said there were efforts to increase OPEC's market share in the global oil market but this seemed to be difficult because of competition from non-OPEC producers.
"I think there is effort to increase OPEC market share, but there is tough competition from non-OPEC producers and also it will depend on the consumers," he said.
OPEC delegates and insiders have said that the recent weakness in crude prices has refocused attention on the rampant violations of mandated OPEC quotas.
For example, member countries told the OPEC headquarters in Vienna last week that production in May was 25.39 million bpd, a 210,000-bpd drop from April, but still above the overall ceiling.
But actual production based on media estimates monitored by OPEC, including a Reuters survey, showed output in May approaching 27 million bpd.
